title: Add overload reason codes + headers to 429 responses
author: Amara Diallo
release_notes:
- Hosted API: 429 responses now include standardized reason codes and headers that distinguish quota limits from overload shedding.
- No behavior change to enforcement in this PR; this is response semantics + logging only.
body:
## Context
Support and customers currently see the same 429 for multiple distinct conditions (quota exceeded, per-minute rate limiting, and new overload shedding / admission control paths). During incidents/bursts this makes it hard to: (a) give correct retry guidance, (b) separate "expected" best-effort shedding from true quota misconfig, and (c) correlate customer complaints with fleet protection triggers.

This PR standardizes 429 semantics (headers + error payload fields) so clients, Support, and on-call can distinguish:
- Quota window exhaustion (account/org quota)
- Rate limit (token bucket / rps) enforcement
- Overload shedding / admission control (capacity protection)

Related: ENG-4922 (tier-aware rate limiter), ENG-4924 (routing admission control). This PR is intentionally scoped to response/reporting so we can ship reason-code clarity ahead of the full GA rollout.

## What changed
### 1) Standard 429 reason taxonomy
Introduces a small, versioned set of reason codes:
- `quota_exceeded` (quota window exceeded)
- `rate_limited` (token bucket / request rate limit)
- `overload_shed` (request rejected due to fleet pressure / admission control)
- `route_budget_exhausted` (per-route budget for the tier depleted)
- `tier_throttled` (best-effort tier throttled due to priority protection)

### 2) Response headers
Adds the following headers to all gateway-generated 429s (and normalizes when upstream returns a 429 without them):
- `x-redwood-error-code`: always `rate_limited` for HTTP 429 (consistent top-level code)
- `x-redwood-429-reason`: one of the reasons above
- `retry-after`: set when we have a meaningful value (quota window remaining, or configured min backoff for overload)
- `x-redwood-request-id`: ensured to be present for all 429 paths (some early-return paths skipped this)

We continue to emit existing `x-ratelimit-*` headers where applicable (no removal).

### 3) Error payload normalization
Ensures the JSON error body includes a stable `code` and a human-readable message that matches the reason:

Example:
{
  "error": {
    "type": "rate_limit_error",
    "code": "overload_shed",
    "message": "Request was throttled due to temporary capacity protection. Retry with exponential backoff.",
    "request_id": "req_..."
  }
}

Notes:
- We did not change the HTTP status code (still 429).
- We did not change which requests are admitted or rejected; only classification + messaging.

### 4) Deterministic logging for support escalation
Adds a structured gateway log field `throttle.reason` and `throttle.retry_after_s` so on-call can quickly answer: "is this quota, or overload?" without reading free-form strings.

## Files / areas touched (high level)
- `services/api-gateway/middleware/throttle_response.ts`: new reason mapping + header writer
- `services/api-gateway/middleware/quota.ts`: propagate quota window retry-after into normalized response
- `services/api-gateway/middleware/admission_control.ts`: set `overload_shed` / `tier_throttled` on reject paths
- `services/api-gateway/openapi/error_schemas.yaml`: updated 429 error code docs + examples
- `services/api-gateway/tests/integration/throttle_reasons.spec.ts`: coverage for each reason + headers

## Test plan
- Added integration tests for each reason that assert:
  - HTTP 429
  - `x-redwood-429-reason` is set and correct
  - `x-redwood-request-id` always present
  - `retry-after` present when applicable
- Manually verified in staging:
  - quota exhaustion path via forced small test quota
  - overload path via admission control test flag (internal only)

## Rollout / compatibility
- Backwards compatible: clients that only look at 429 continue to work.
- New behavior is additive (new headers + stable code strings).
- Docs updates for customers will land in a separate docs PR (Wei/Elliot are tracking in ENG-4930).

## Follow-ups
- Wire `route_budget_exhausted` reason from routing service (currently only gateway-originated budgets emit it).
- Ensure Console surfaces these reasons in internal operator view (tracked separately).

Refs:
- Jira: SUP-18421 (customer confusion during rollout), SUP-18462 (streaming termination confusion; separate fix PR)
- Project: Hot-route capacity protection
commits: api-gateway: introduce ThrottleReason enum and mapping helpers
api-gateway: normalize 429 headers + payload across early-return paths
api-gateway: add integration tests for quota vs overload reason codes
review_comments: Jordan Lee (requested changes): Can we keep the top-level `x-redwood-error-code` stable and put the detailed classification in a separate header? Some internal tooling keys off `rate_limited` today.

Amara Diallo (author): Yep—updated to always use `x-redwood-error-code=rate_limited` for HTTP 429 and added `x-redwood-429-reason` for the detailed code. Also ensured JSON payload `error.code` matches the reason.
Dev Patel: Please make sure Support can tell customers exactly what to do. Can we include explicit retry guidance in the message for overload vs quota?
Amara Diallo (author): Added reason-specific messages (quota: "increase quota or wait", overload: "retry with exponential backoff"). Also ensured `retry-after` is set when we have a concrete value.
Logan Wright: Any risk of high-cardinality logging here? Please avoid logging tenant IDs in the throttle log line.

Amara Diallo (author): Logs only include reason + retry_after_s + request_id and route group; tenant/account identifiers remain in existing auth log context (unchanged). No new high-cardinality dimensions added.
Kaitlyn Nguyen: Header naming: prefer `x-redwood-429-reason` vs `x-redwood-throttle-reason`? Consistency with other error headers matters.
Amara Diallo (author): Settled on `x-redwood-429-reason` to be explicit and avoid ambiguity with non-429 throttling. OpenAPI examples updated accordingly.
